title: Overview and justification
body:
This course is about citing sources in your own work: bringing them in accurately, building a reference list that holds up, and applying a referencing style with purpose. You already know what referencing is and why it matters. This course is about doing it well.

Citation is a practical skill you use in almost every assignment. Quote or paraphrase a source and you must cite it; list that source correctly at the end; keep one style across the whole piece. Get this right and your work reads as careful, honest and well researched, and it earns marks against the criteria.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: integrate sources into your writing using in-text citation, through quotation and paraphrase
construct accurate references for a range of source types
apply a referencing style consistently and use citation to evidence your work against marking criteria.

title: In real academic practice
body: Citation runs through everything you write at university. Every essay that draws on reading, every report that cites data, every dissertation with a reference list, depends on citing sources accurately and consistently. Getting it right protects your academic integrity and shows a marker the scope of your research. The same care carries into professional work, where sourcing a claim well is part of being trusted.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, citing as you write: quoting and paraphrasing a source, with the citation in the right place. Second, building accurate references: assembling a reference for a book, a journal article and a web page. Third, working with referencing styles: choosing one, applying it consistently, and using citation to meet marking criteria. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Orientation
body: You have a source that supports your point, and you want to use it in an essay. You have two choices: quote the author's exact words, or put the idea into your own words and paraphrase it. Either way, you must tell the reader where it came from, with an in-text citation. This lesson is about making those moves well.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are not just recognising a citation when you see one; you are producing citations in your own writing. The aim is to choose quotation or paraphrase on purpose, place the citation correctly, and paraphrase without slipping into the author's own wording. These are the moves your assignments now expect.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: choose between quotation and paraphrase to bring a source into your writing
place an in-text citation correctly when you quote and when you paraphrase
paraphrase a source from {{context}} accurately in your own words and cite it.

title: Concept: definition
body:
An in-text citation is a short note, in brackets, that credits the source of an idea at the point you use it. In the author-date style this is the author's surname and the year, with a page number when you quote, such as (Okafor, 2021, p.44). It points the reader to the full reference in your list.

You have two ways to bring a source in. Quoting reproduces the author's exact words inside quotation marks. Paraphrasing puts the author's point into your own words. Paraphrasing is the more skilful move, because it shows you have understood the idea, not just copied it. Both ways need an in-text citation.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about the last time you used a source in an assignment. Did you quote it or paraphrase it, and was the citation in the right place? What would you do differently now?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Bringing a source into your writing means choosing quotation or paraphrase, and citing it either way. Quote the exact words, in quotation marks and with a page number, when the precise wording matters. Paraphrase, in your own words, to show you have understood, which is the move markers reward most. Place the citation next to the idea it supports. The next lesson builds the full reference that each citation points to.

title: Orientation
body: Every in-text citation points to a full reference in your list at the end of the work. A reference is built from a fixed set of elements, in a set order, and a marker expects to find them all, correctly arranged. This lesson is about assembling an accurate reference for the sources you use most.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are constructing references yourself, not just recognising one. The aim is to know the elements a reference needs, put them in the right order for each source type, and avoid the small errors that creep in when you let software build the reference for you.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: identify the elements a reference is built from and the order they take
construct a reference for a book, a journal article and a web page
spot and fix the inaccuracies that come from copying a reference in {{context}} out of a database.

title: Concept: definition
body:
A reference gives the reader everything they need to find the source. For a book in the author-date style, the elements are: author surname and initial; year of publication, in brackets; title and any subtitle, in italics; place of publication; and publisher. They always appear in that order.

Different source types need slightly different elements. A journal article adds the article title, the journal name, the volume and issue, and the page range. A web page adds the web address and the date you accessed it. The order is fixed, so once you know the pattern you can build a reference for almost any source.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Look back at a reference list you have written. Did you build the references yourself, or paste them from a database? Pick one entry and check it against the pattern.
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: A reference is built from a fixed set of elements in a set order: for a book, author, year, title, place and publisher. A journal article and a web page use the same logic with a few elements of their own. Build each reference yourself from the pattern, rather than trusting a database to do it, and check it before it goes in your list. The next lesson is about the style that sets these patterns, and applying it consistently.

title: Orientation
body: The patterns you have been using belong to one referencing style: the author-date, or Harvard, style. Other styles exist, and your discipline usually settles which one you use. Whichever it is, the rule is the same: apply it consistently across the whole piece. This lesson is about choosing a style and using citation to earn marks.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are not inventing a style; you are selecting the right one and applying it without slips. The aim is to recognise the main style families, keep one style consistently through a piece of work, and understand how a good reference list evidences your research to a marker.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: select a referencing style suited to your discipline and apply it consistently
explain how citation evidences your research against marking criteria
use citation to show the scope and critical edge of your reading in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
A referencing style is an agreed set of rules for how citations and references are laid out. The most common in UK universities is author-date, usually called Harvard. Others include APA, used in psychology and the social sciences; Vancouver, used in medical subjects; and OSCOLA, used in law. Your department will tell you which to use.

The style you use matters less than using it consistently. A marker reads your reference list to judge the scope of your research, and often turns to it first. Accurate, consistent citation signals that you have read widely and engaged with your sources, which is exactly what the marking criteria reward.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Which referencing style does your subject use, and how consistently have you applied it? Find one slip in a recent piece of work and note how you would correct it.
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: A referencing style is a set of rules for laying out citations and references, and your discipline usually decides which one you use. Harvard is the common author-date style; APA, Vancouver and OSCOLA serve particular subjects. What matters most is consistency: one style, applied to every citation and reference. Done well, your reference list shows a marker the scope and care of your research, and earns marks against the criteria. You can now cite, reference and apply a style with purpose.

title: Course Sources
instruction: This course draws on the following source.

_items.title: See pages 188 to 198 of Chapter 10, 'Academic Integrity and Referencing', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Explore the concept
body: Four cards on bringing a source into your writing. Review each one.
instruction: Read through the cards below.

_items.title: Quoting
_items.subtitle: The author's exact words
_items.text: Reproduce the wording exactly, inside quotation marks, with a page number in the citation. Quote when the precise phrasing matters, such as a definition or a striking line. Keep quotations short and few.

_items.title: Paraphrasing
_items.subtitle: The idea in your words
_items.text: Restate the author's point in your own words and sentence shape. Paraphrase to show you have understood the idea and to keep your own voice. It is the move markers reward most.

_items.title: When to cite
_items.subtitle: Every borrowed idea
_items.text: Cite every time you use a source, whether you quote or paraphrase. If an idea, a fact or an argument is not your own, it needs a citation. When in doubt, cite.

_items.title: Where it goes
_items.subtitle: Next to the idea
_items.text: Place the citation next to the idea it supports, usually at the end of the sentence before the full stop. A reader should be in no doubt which claim came from which source.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students want to use the same sentence from a source: 'Regular low-stakes testing improves long-term retention' (Okafor, 2021, p.44).

{{learner-a}} writes: Okafor (2021) says that regular low-stakes testing improves long-term retention. The wording is almost identical to the original, but there are no quotation marks. It reads as {{learner-a}}'s own phrasing of a borrowed sentence, so it is neither a clean paraphrase nor a quotation. The citation is there, but the move is muddled.

{{learner-b}} writes: testing yourself often, in ways that do not count for marks, helps you hold on to what you learn (Okafor, 2021). The idea is kept, the words are {{learner-b}}'s own, and the source is cited. Where the exact phrasing mattered, {{learner-b}} could instead quote it directly: 'regular low-stakes testing improves long-term retention' (Okafor, 2021, p.44).

Both students used the source. Only {{learner-b}} made a clean choice between paraphrase and quotation, and cited it correctly.

title: Citing a source
body: Use these questions each time you bring a source into your writing.
instruction: Tick each item once you have checked it.

_items.text: Have I decided whether to quote or paraphrase, and why?
If I quoted, did I use the author's exact words inside quotation marks?
If I quoted, did I include a page number in the citation?
If I paraphrased, are the words and sentence shape genuinely my own?
Have I placed an in-text citation next to the idea it supports?
Could a reader trace every borrowed idea back to a source?

title: Formative check: quotation and paraphrase
displayTitle: Which statement best describes the difference between quoting and paraphrasing?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the difference between quoting and paraphrasing?

_items.text: Quoting reproduces the author's exact words in quotation marks; paraphrasing restates the idea in your own words.
_items.feedback: Yes. Quotation keeps the exact wording; paraphrase puts the idea into your own words.

_items.text: Quoting needs a citation, but paraphrasing does not.
_items.feedback: Both quotation and paraphrase need an in-text citation.

_items.text: Paraphrasing means changing a few of the author's words here and there.
_items.feedback: That is too close to the original. A paraphrase restates the idea in genuinely new words.

_items.text: Quoting and paraphrasing are two names for the same thing.
_items.feedback: They are different moves: one keeps the exact words, the other restates the idea.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Quotation keeps the author's exact words in quotation marks; paraphrase restates the idea in your own words.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what each move does with the author's actual words.
_incorrect.final: Quoting reproduces the exact words in quotation marks; paraphrasing restates the idea in your own words. Both still need a citation.

title: Formative check: placing the citation
displayTitle: In the worked example, why did the stronger version give a page number in one citation but not the other?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why did the stronger version give a page number in only one citation?

_items.text: A page number is given with a direct quotation, but a paraphrase needs only the author and year.
_items.feedback: Yes. Quote with a page number; paraphrase with author and year.

_items.text: Page numbers are optional and the student added one at random.
_items.feedback: Page numbers are not random: they go with a direct quotation.

_items.text: A paraphrase needs a page number, but a quotation does not.
_items.feedback: It is the other way round: the quotation is what needs the page number.

_items.text: Neither citation really needed a page number.
_items.feedback: The direct quotation needs a page number so the reader can find the exact words.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A direct quotation carries a page number; a paraphrase cites author and year.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at which version quoted the exact words, and which restated the idea.
_incorrect.final: The direct quotation carries a page number so the reader can find the exact words; the paraphrase needs only author and year.

title: Formative check: paraphrasing and citing
displayTitle: You are paraphrasing a key source in {{context}}. Which approach produces an acceptable paraphrase with a correct citation?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which approach is an acceptable paraphrase with a correct citation?

_items.text: Restate the author's point in your own words and sentence shape, with an author-date citation.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is a clean paraphrase in {{context}}, properly cited.

_items.text: Copy the sentence and change two or three words, with no citation.
_items.feedback: Changing a few words is too close to the original, and it still needs a citation.

_items.text: Put the author's exact words in your sentence without quotation marks.
_items.feedback: Exact words without quotation marks read as your own: that is not an honest paraphrase.

_items.text: Restate the idea well in your own words, but leave out the citation.
_items.feedback: A good paraphrase still needs an in-text citation crediting the source.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A paraphrase in {{context}} restates the idea in your own words and still carries an author-date citation.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. A clean paraphrase uses your own words AND credits the source.
_incorrect.final: An acceptable paraphrase restates the point in your own words and sentence shape, with an author-date citation. The other options copy wording or drop the citation.

title: Explore the concept
body: The elements of a book reference, in the order they take. Reveal each stage to build the reference.
instruction: Select each stage to reveal the next element.

_items.title: Author
_items.body: Start with the author's surname, then their initial: Dancer, R. The surname comes first so the list can be ordered alphabetically.

_items.title: Year
_items.body: Add the year of publication in brackets: (2020). This is the date your in-text citation matches.

_items.title: Title
_items.body: Give the title, and any subtitle, in italics: Writing with sources. Capitalise only the first word and any proper nouns.

_items.title: Place
_items.body: Name the place of publication: London. This is the town or city, not the country.

_items.title: Publisher
_items.body: End with the publisher: Camlann Press. The finished reference reads: Dancer, R. (2020) Writing with sources. London: Camlann Press.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students reference the same book in their essays.

{{learner-a}} copies the reference straight from the library database: DANCER, Rhys. Writing With Sources. 2020. Camlann Press. The elements are mostly there, but the order and formatting are wrong. The first name is spelled out, the title is over-capitalised, the year sits in the wrong place, and the place of publication is missing. This is what copying from a database often produces.

{{learner-b}} builds the reference by hand from the pattern: Dancer, R. (2020) Writing with sources. London: Camlann Press. Surname then initial, year in brackets, title in italics, then place and publisher. It is accurate, consistent, and ready for an alphabetical list.

Both students had the same book. Only {{learner-b}}'s reference would pass a marker's eye.

title: Building a reference
body: Check each reference you build against these points.
instruction: Tick each item once you have checked it.

_items.text: Have I put the author's surname first, then the initial?
Is the year in brackets, matching my in-text citation?
Is the title in italics, with only the first word and proper nouns capitalised?
For a journal article, have I added the journal name, volume, issue and page range?
For a web page, have I added the web address and the date I accessed it?
Have I built the reference myself, rather than pasting it from a database?

title: Formative check: the order of elements
displayTitle: In the author-date style, which is the correct order of elements for a book reference?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which is the correct order of elements for a book reference?

_items.text: Author surname and initial, year in brackets, title in italics, place of publication, publisher.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is the fixed order for a book reference.

_items.text: Title, author, publisher, year, place of publication.
_items.feedback: The author comes first, not the title, and the year follows the author.

_items.text: Author full first name and surname, publisher, title, year.
_items.feedback: Use the initial, not the full first name, and the year follows the author in brackets.

_items.text: Year, title, author surname, place of publication.
_items.feedback: The author surname comes first so the list can be ordered alphabetically.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Author and initial, year in brackets, title in italics, place, then publisher.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Remember the list is ordered by author, so the surname comes first.
_incorrect.final: The order is author surname and initial, year in brackets, title in italics, place of publication, then publisher.

title: Formative check: accurate versus copied
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's reference accurate where the first student's was not?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's reference accurate?

_items.text: It followed the fixed order and formatting: surname then initial, year in brackets, title in italics, place and publisher.
_items.feedback: Yes. Building from the pattern kept every element right.

_items.text: It was copied more carefully from the same database.
_items.feedback: It was not copied at all: the student built it by hand from the pattern.

_items.text: It used more of the author's full name and capital letters.
_items.feedback: The full first name and extra capitals were the first student's errors.

_items.text: It left out the place of publication to keep things simple.
_items.feedback: The place of publication belongs in the reference; leaving it out is an error.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second reference followed the fixed order and formatting exactly.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Compare how each reference handled the order and the formatting of the elements.
_incorrect.final: The second reference was accurate because it followed the fixed order and formatting, built by hand from the pattern rather than copied.

title: Formative check: fixing a copied reference
displayTitle: You copy a reference for a {{context}} source straight from your library's database. What should you do before putting it in your list?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What should you do with a reference copied from a database?

_items.text: Check it against the correct pattern and fix the order, capitalisation and any missing elements.
_items.feedback: Yes. A copied reference in {{context}} almost always needs checking and fixing.

_items.text: Trust it, because the library database is the authoritative source.
_items.feedback: Databases often introduce errors, so a copied reference cannot be trusted as it stands.

_items.text: Delete the author so the entry stays short.
_items.feedback: The author is essential: the list is ordered by it and the citation points to it.

_items.text: Change the style to a numbered one so the errors do not show.
_items.feedback: Switching style does not fix the errors, and it breaks consistency with the rest of your list.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Check a copied reference in {{context}} against the pattern and fix whatever is wrong before it goes in your list.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Remember why copying references from a database is risky.
_incorrect.final: A copied reference should be checked against the correct pattern and fixed for order, capitalisation and missing elements before it goes in your list.

title: Explore the concept
body: The main families of referencing style, and the rule that matters most. Read each tab.
instruction: Select each tab to read about that style.

_items.title: Author-date (Harvard)
_items.body: The author's surname and the year appear in the text, with a full reference in an alphabetical list. It is used widely across many disciplines, and is the default in most UK universities.

_items.title: APA
_items.body: An author-date style with its own rules, used in psychology, the social sciences and some business subjects. It is close to Harvard, but the details differ, so do not mix the two in one piece.

_items.title: Vancouver and OSCOLA
_items.body: Numbered styles, where a number in the text points to a reference. Vancouver is used in medical and clinical subjects; OSCOLA, a footnote style, is used in law.

_items.title: The real rule: consistency
_items.body: Whichever style your discipline uses, apply it to every citation and every reference in the piece. One style, followed exactly, matters more than which style you chose.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students hand in essays, each with a reference list.

{{learner-a}} has read widely, but the reference list mixes styles. Some entries give the year in brackets and others do not; some titles are in italics and others in quotation marks; one citation uses a number. The marker cannot tell at a glance how carefully the sources were handled, and the inconsistency undercuts otherwise good research.

{{learner-b}} has read the same sources and used one style, Harvard, throughout. Every citation matches a full reference, every reference follows the same pattern, and the list is alphabetical. The marker sees the scope of the reading at once, and the consistency reads as care and competence.

Both students did the reading. Only {{learner-b}}'s citation let the marker see it.

title: Applying a style
body: Run through these points before you hand in a piece of work.
instruction: Tick each item once you have checked it.

_items.text: Do I know which referencing style my department requires?
Have I used that one style for every citation and reference?
Does every in-text citation have a matching entry in the reference list?
Is my reference list in the order the style requires, usually alphabetical?
Does my reference list show the range of sources I actually read?
Have I checked the list for stray entries in a different style?

title: Formative check: applying a style
displayTitle: Your department requires the Harvard style. What matters most when you apply it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What matters most when you apply a required style?

_items.text: Using it consistently, so every citation and reference follows the same pattern.
_items.feedback: Yes. Consistency across the whole piece matters most.

_items.text: Using Harvard for some sources and a numbered style for the harder ones.
_items.feedback: Mixing styles breaks consistency; use the one required style throughout.

_items.text: Choosing whichever style makes your list look shortest.
_items.feedback: The style is set by your department, not chosen for appearance.

_items.text: Switching style partway through if you run out of time.
_items.feedback: A piece of work should keep one style from start to finish.

_feedback.correct: That's right. What matters most is applying the required style consistently across every citation and reference.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. The style is already decided for you, so what is left in your control?
_incorrect.final: What matters most is consistency: using the one required style for every citation and reference in the piece.

title: Formative check: what the list signalled
displayTitle: In the worked example, why did the second student's reference list work in their favour with the marker?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why did the second student's reference list work in their favour?

_items.text: One consistent style let the marker see the scope of the reading at a glance.
_items.feedback: Yes. Consistency made the research easy to read and judge.

_items.text: It listed more sources than the first student's.
_items.feedback: Both students read the same sources; the difference was consistency, not number.

_items.text: It used an unusual style that stood out.
_items.feedback: A standard, consistent style helped; an unusual one would not.

_items.text: It placed the references at the start of the essay.
_items.feedback: The position was not the point; the consistency of the list was.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A single consistent style let the marker take in the scope of the reading at once.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Both students read the same sources, so what made the difference?
_incorrect.final: The second list worked because one consistent style let the marker see the scope of the reading at a glance.

title: Formative check: what citation signals
displayTitle: A marker turns to your reference list first in a {{context}} essay. What does a full, consistent list signal to them?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does a full, consistent reference list signal to a marker?

_items.text: The scope of your research and the critical edge of your reading.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, a strong list shows how widely and carefully you read.

_items.text: That you spent a long time formatting the document.
_items.feedback: It signals the research behind the work, not time spent on layout.

_items.text: Nothing in particular, since markers ignore reference lists.
_items.feedback: Markers often read the reference list first, precisely because it tells them a lot.

_items.text: That you prefer one style over another.
_items.feedback: It signals the scope and quality of your reading, not a style preference.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, a full, consistent reference list signals the scope and critical edge of your research.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about why a marker reads the reference list first.
_incorrect.final: A full, consistent reference list signals the scope of your research and the critical edge of your reading, which is why markers read it first.

body: When should you use a direct quotation rather than a paraphrase?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: When should you quote rather than paraphrase?

_items.text: When the author's exact wording matters, such as a precise definition or a striking phrase.
_items.feedback: Yes. Quote when the exact words carry the point.

_items.text: Whenever you are short of time to rewrite the idea.
_items.feedback: Quoting is not a shortcut for paraphrasing.

_items.text: Whenever you want to fill more of the word count.
_items.feedback: Length is not a reason to quote.

_items.text: Every time you use a source, as a rule.
_items.feedback: Most of the time a paraphrase is the better move.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Quote when the author's exact wording matters.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about when the exact words, rather than the idea, are what count.

body: You put an author's idea into your own words for an essay. What must you still do?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What must you do when you paraphrase an idea?

_items.text: Add an in-text citation crediting the source.
_items.feedback: Yes. A paraphrase still needs a citation.

_items.text: Nothing, because the words are now your own.
_items.feedback: The idea is still the author's, so it needs a citation.

_items.text: Put the whole sentence in quotation marks.
_items.feedback: Quotation marks are for exact wording, not a paraphrase.

_items.text: Add a page number but no author.
_items.feedback: A citation needs the author and year, not a bare page number.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A paraphrase still needs an in-text citation.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. The idea still belongs to the author, even in your own words.

body: In the author-date style, which is the correct order of elements for a book reference?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which is the correct order for a book reference?

_items.text: Author surname and initial, year in brackets, title in italics, place of publication, publisher.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is the fixed order.

_items.text: Title, author, year, publisher, place of publication.
_items.feedback: The author comes first, not the title.

_items.text: Author surname and initial, title, publisher, year.
_items.feedback: The year follows the author, in brackets.

_items.text: Publisher, place of publication, author, year, title.
_items.feedback: The author surname comes first so the list can be alphabetised.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Author and initial, year, title, place, then publisher.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Remember the list is ordered by author.

body: Why is it risky to paste a reference straight from a library database into your list?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is pasting a reference from a database risky?

_items.text: Databases often introduce errors in order, capitalisation and missing elements.
_items.feedback: Yes. Copied references usually need checking and fixing.

_items.text: Databases never include the author's name.
_items.feedback: They usually include the author; the problem is errors and formatting.

_items.text: It is faster to retype the whole reference from memory.
_items.feedback: The issue is accuracy, not speed.

_items.text: Pasted references are always in the wrong language.
_items.feedback: Language is not the issue; accuracy and formatting are.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Database references often carry errors, so they need checking.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what tends to go wrong with a copied reference.

body: Your department requires one referencing style. What matters most when you apply it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What matters most when applying a required style?

_items.text: Using one style consistently across every citation and reference.
_items.feedback: Yes. Consistency matters most.

_items.text: Mixing styles so the list looks varied.
_items.feedback: Mixing styles breaks consistency.

_items.text: Choosing the style that gives the shortest entries.
_items.feedback: The style is set by the department, not chosen for length.

_items.text: Changing style for sources you find harder to reference.
_items.feedback: One style should run through the whole piece.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Apply the one required style consistently throughout.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. The style is already decided, so what is in your control?

body: Why do markers often turn to your reference list first?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why do markers read the reference list first?

_items.text: It shows the scope and quality of the research behind the work.
_items.feedback: Yes. The list reveals how widely and carefully you read.

_items.text: It is the easiest part of the essay to ignore.
_items.feedback: Markers read it precisely because it tells them a lot.

_items.text: It shows how long the essay took to write.
_items.feedback: It signals research, not time spent.

_items.text: It is where the marks are added up.
_items.feedback: Marks are not totalled in the reference list; it signals the research.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The reference list shows the scope and quality of your research.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what a reference list tells a marker about your reading.

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: citing a source as you write, building an accurate reference for it, and applying one referencing style consistently. On their own they are three separate ideas. This lesson brings them together into one practice you can keep using.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are not expected to reference like an expert. The aim is to see these three as one connected practice, not three separate jobs, so it carries on past this course and into your later studies.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: connect in-text citation, accurate references and a consistent style as one referencing practice
apply the three together as one referencing practice on a student's whole assignment
analyse how in-text citation, accurate references and a consistent style work as one across your {{context}} assignments

title: Concept: definition
body: Referencing is one connected practice, not three separate jobs done at different times. When you bring a source in, you place a citation; that citation must point to an accurate reference in your list; and both follow one consistent style. The three ideas from the earlier lessons are the parts of that single practice, and they lock together across a whole piece of work.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, this means handling sources the same connected way on every piece of work, in any subject. You choose a style, cite each source as you write, build a matching reference, and keep the whole list consistent. The in-text citation and the reference list are two ends of one thread, held together by the style. Doing all three as one practice, on every assignment, is what keeps your referencing accurate.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about an assignment you have coming up. How will you run referencing as one practice on it, from choosing a style to the final consistency check, and where will you start?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Referencing is most useful when you treat it as one connected practice, not three separate jobs. You run the same parts in order on every piece: choose a style, cite each source, build a matching reference, and check the whole list is consistent. It is handling all three as one practice, assignment after assignment, that keeps your referencing accurate.

title: The steps as one process
body: Referencing runs as one connected sequence across a whole piece of work. Select each step to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each step.

_items.title: Choose a style
_items.body: Choose a referencing style suited to your subject before you start writing.

_items.title: Cite sources
_items.body: As you write, bring each source in by quoting or paraphrasing, and place an in-text citation.

_items.title: Build references
_items.body: Build an accurate full reference for each source you cited, following that style.

_items.title: Check and submit
_items.body: Check that every citation matches a reference and the whole list keeps one style, then hand it in.

title: Worked example
body: Two students each write a piece that draws on several sources. One treats referencing as separate jobs: they cite as they go, but build the list in a rush at the end, and it mixes styles and misses entries. The other runs it as one practice: one style chosen first, each source cited and given a matching reference, and a final check of the whole list. Both read the same sources, but only the second student's referencing holds together under a marker's eye.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: Checklist: How to reference across a whole piece
body: Use these to check your referencing holds together as one practice, not three separate jobs.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Did I choose one referencing style and use it throughout?
Did I cite every source I quoted or paraphrased, at the point I used it?
Does every in-text citation have a matching reference in my list?
Did I build each reference accurately from the pattern, rather than paste it in?
Will I run this same referencing practice on my next assignment?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to treat referencing as one connected practice rather than three separate jobs?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to treat referencing as one connected practice rather than three separate jobs?

_items.text: Because each part depends on the next: a citation points to a reference, and one consistent style holds both together across the piece.
_items.feedback: Yes. The parts connect, so handling them as one practice keeps your referencing accurate.

_items.text: Because getting one part right means you can skip the other two.
_items.feedback: No. The parts connect, so one cannot stand in for the rest.

_items.text: Because it means you never have to build a reference list.
_items.feedback: Not so. The reference list is part of the one practice, not something it removes.

_items.text: Because one practice takes less thought than learning three separate jobs.
_items.feedback: The gain is not less thought. It is that the parts feed one another.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Referencing is one practice whose parts depend on one another, run across the whole piece.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how a citation, a reference and a style connect.

displayTitle: A student chooses one style, cites each source as they write by quoting or paraphrasing, builds a matching reference for each, and checks the list is consistent before handing in. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student chooses one style, cites each source as they write by quoting or paraphrasing, builds a matching reference for each, and checks the list is consistent before handing in. What does this show?

_items.text: That the student is using referencing as one practice: each part connects, from the citation to the reference to the consistent style.
_items.feedback: Yes. Every part is there, connected, working as one practice.

_items.text: That the student is doing far more than any piece of work needs.
_items.feedback: No. Each part does a different job, and together they make the referencing sound.

_items.text: That only the final check at the end really matters.
_items.feedback: Not so. The earlier parts did the real work; the check only confirms it.

_items.text: That citing and building references are the same step.
_items.feedback: They are different parts: you cite as you write, and build the full reference for the list.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The student ran the whole practice, each part connecting to the next.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Notice how the student moves through every part and ties them together.

displayTitle: You want to use this whole referencing practice to handle sources in your {{context}} work this term. Which plan best treats referencing as one connected practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to use this whole referencing practice to handle sources in your your subject work this term. Which plan best treats referencing as one connected practice?

_items.text: Pick one style, cite each source as you write, build a matching reference for each, and check the list is consistent before handing in.
_items.feedback: Yes. That runs every part of the practice, in order, on each piece.

_items.text: Leave all the referencing until the night before, then paste a list together from your databases.
_items.feedback: That breaks the practice: citations and references drift apart and the style slips.

_items.text: Only reference the sources you quote directly, and leave the paraphrased ones out.
_items.feedback: Every source you use needs a citation and a reference, whether you quoted or paraphrased.

_items.text: Use whichever style looks easiest for each source as you go.
_items.feedback: Mixing styles breaks consistency, which is what holds the practice together.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Running every part across the whole piece is referencing as one practice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the plan that connects every part and keeps one style.
